1.title: The Progress Practice in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: The Progress Practice in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. three point seven.one apply the progress practice: key management products, areas of focus of the key roles, effective management and techniques. three point seven.two analyze whether an approach to progress is effective and fit for purpose, using the principles, the techniques and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (fifty-one percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. The progress practice gives the project a way to monitor actual results against the plan, to forecast the objectives and continued viability, and to control deviations that are not acceptable. Good control answers three questions at every level: where are we, where will we end up, and what must change?

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. The figure shows this: Progress control at four levels, with tolerances and escalation running from the team manager to the project manager, the project board and the corporate level.

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. It serves manage by exception (tolerances and escalation), manage by stages (decision points at stage ends), ensure continued business justification (forecasts show whether the case holds), learn from experience (lessons captured as they appear) and focus on products (progress measured by products delivered, not hours spent). Exam tip: Progress is about forecasting, not only reporting. An approach that tells the board where the stage will end is stronger than one that only describes what has happened.

1.title: The key management products
1.text: The key management products. Daily log (project log). The project manager's informal notes, actions and decisions. Lessons log (project log). Running record of lessons from this project and earlier ones. Lessons report. Passes lessons on for others to use. Checkpoint report. Team manager to project manager: one work package, at the agreed interval. Highlight report. Project manager to board: stage progress and forecast, at the agreed interval. End stage report. Project manager to board at a stage end: results, the case, the risks, the next stage.

1.title: The key management products, continued
1.text: The key management products. Exception report. Project manager to board when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: cause, options, recommendation. End project report. Project manager to board: performance against the P I D and the business case. Digital and data management approach (P I D). How data and digital tools are used, shared and protected. Exam tip: A checkpoint report goes from the team manager to the project manager. Highlight, end stage, exception and end project reports go from the project manager to the board. A team manager who reports to the board breaks the reporting line.

1.title: Roles and areas of focus
1.text: Roles and areas of focus. The roles follow the levels of management. Learn each focus, and check the Official Book's table for the exact wording. Executive. Uses reports and forecasts to confirm the project is still justified. Senior user and senior supplier. Review progress for their own interest: user readiness, supplier delivery. Project manager. Monitors the stage; keeps the logs; writes highlight, end stage and exception reports; forecasts and escalates.

1.title: Roles and areas of focus, continued
1.text: Roles and areas of focus. Team manager. Agrees work package tolerances; sends checkpoint reports; escalates to the project manager. Project assurance. Independently checks that progress information is reliable. Project support. Runs the reporting tools and keeps the logs and data tidy.

1.title: Effective management and techniques
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Exam tip: Each level sets tolerances for the level below. The board sets stage tolerances; the project manager sets work package tolerances.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Tolerances can cover time, cost, quality, scope, benefits, risk and sustainability, not only time and cost. Corporate or programme. Sets the project tolerances; receives escalation if the board forecasts a breach. Project board. Sets the stage tolerances; reads highlight reports; decides on exception reports. Project manager. Sets work package tolerances; controls the stage day to day; escalates exceptions. Team manager. Works within the work package tolerances; sends checkpoint reports.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. A good approach uses time-driven and event-driven controls together. Time-driven. Board level: Highlight reports at the agreed interval. Project manager level: Checkpoint reports; regular review of logs and registers. Event-driven. Board level: Stage decisions, ad hoc direction, exception reports. Project manager level: Authorizing and accepting work packages; escalating events.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Review and report. Compare actual with plan, products first, at an interval that fits the stage's length and risk. Forecast. Estimate where time, cost and benefits will end up, and report the trend. Escalate. When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, send an exception report at once, with cause, options and a recommendation. Learn. Record lessons as they appear and review them at each stage end. Use data well. Keep one protected source of progress data, as the digital and data management approach sets out. Exam tip: When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, the project manager escalates at once. The project manager does not decide alone and does not wait for the next report. The board then decides, for example by asking for an exception plan.

1.title: Judging a progress approach
1.text: Judging a progress approach. Report interval fits the stage and its risk. One fixed interval for every stage (manage by stages). Right detail: team detail to the project manager, summary and forecast to the board. The board receives team-level detail (define roles). Tolerances set at each level and used in reports. No stage tolerance, or never mentioned (manage by exception). Forecasts with trends and the effect on the case. Reports only what is done; problems found at stage end (business justification).

1.title: Judging a progress approach, continued
1.text: Judging a progress approach. Exceptions escalated early with options. A forecast breach hidden or held for the next report (manage by exception). Lessons captured continuously. Lessons gathered only at the end (learn from experience). Progress measured by products. Progress measured by effort or time elapsed (focus on products). Data and tools agreed and protected. Inconsistent spreadsheets; sensitive data shared freely.

2.title: Judging a progress approach, continued
2.text: Judging a progress approach. Tailoring changes the form of progress control, never the need for it. Agile team. Task boards, stand-ups and iteration reviews can serve as checkpoint information if the work package agrees; the project manager still forecasts to the board. Small project. Short, informal reports and fewer events; the board keeps its decision points and tolerances. Large or multi-supplier project. Common templates; supplier reporting written into contracts. Sustainability, digital and data concerns. Sustainability measures and data protection added to tolerances and reports. Exam tip: A tailored approach still forecasts, sets tolerances and escalates exceptions. If an option drops one of these because the project is small or agile, it is not tailoring.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. In the build stage of Project Harbor, the stage cost tolerance is plus or minus ten percent. Sam Okafor, the project manager, forecasts cost fourteen percent over and sends an exception report to the board that day. Was this an appropriate action, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because a forecast breach of stage tolerance should reach the board immediately. A forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception that must be escalated at once; the project tolerance is not Sam's to use.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. On Project Harbor, Sam has recorded no lessons during the build stage because the team is busy. He plans to collect them all for the end project report. Was this an appropriate approach, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because lessons belong in the lessons log as they appear and are reviewed each stage. Learn from experience means capturing lessons continuously in the lessons log and reviewing them at stage ends, not leaving them to the end.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Sam is about to authorize a work package for Wei Chen's development team on Project Harbor. Who sets the tolerances for this work package? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Sam Okafor, the project manager, within the stage tolerances. Each level sets tolerances for the level below, so the project manager sets work package tolerances inside the stage tolerances set by the board.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Project Harbor's build stage lasts four months and carries a high delivery risk. Sam sends highlight reports monthly, and the board saw a slip only at the stage end. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Agree a shorter highlight report interval and add forecasts to each report. The interval should fit the stage's length and risk and a forecast lets the board act early, while checkpoint reports go to the project manager.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Wei Chen's team works in two-week iterations with a visible task board and daily stand-ups. Sam asked for weekly written checkpoint reports, and the team says the board already shows progress. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Agree in the work package that the task board and stand-ups serve as checkpoint information. Tailoring may change the form of checkpoint information as long as the reporting need and the tolerances stay in place.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Jon Park, project support, asks which management product should state the tools that hold Project Harbor's progress data, who may see the data and how it is protected. Which product should he use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The digital and data management approach in the P I D. The digital and data management approach covers tools, access and protection of project data, while the communication approach covers who is told what.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is an exception? Answer: A situation where a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Question two. Who sends a checkpoint report, and who receives it? Answer: The team manager sends it to the project manager. Question three. Name the two types of control and give one example of each. Answer: Time-driven, such as the highlight report; event-driven, such as the exception report.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Who sets the stage tolerances? Answer: The project board, for the project manager. Question five. What does the daily log hold? Answer: The project manager's informal notes, actions and decisions not held in other products. Question six. Which report reviews the whole project against the P I D and the business case? Answer: The end project report.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Purpose: monitor, forecast and control deviations. Tolerance levels: corporate sets project, board sets stage, project manager sets work package. Controls: time-driven and event-driven, used together. Reports: checkpoint to the project manager. Escalation: at once, when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Effective approach: right interval, forecasts, tolerances used, early escalation, continuous lessons. Tailoring: change the form, keep forecasting, tolerances and escalation.
